newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds close mixed in light trading.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds close mixed in light trading.

text.p: Canadian bonds closed mostly mixed in light trading on Friday as nervous investors sold short-end positions on news of a sharp drop in Canada's unemployment rate and renewed fears of interest rate hikes, analysts said.
Statistics Canada reported the unemployment rate dropped to 9.1 percent in June from 9.5 percent in May. A Reuters poll of economists had forecast a drop to 9.3 percent in June.
Canada's employment growth increased by 51,500 in June, slightly below May's figure of 61,000 but above market expectations of an increase of 38,800.
"The stronger-than-expected employment data clearly has the market looking for another rate hike from the Bank of Canada," said Rob Palombi, fixed-income analyst with Toronto-based MMS International.
"As a result, the front end (of the curve) took it on the chin," Palombi said.
Canada's 10-year benchmark bond rose C$0.04 to C$109.30 to yield 5.988 percent, compared to its U.S. equivalent which climbed 6/32 to yield 6.23 percent.
The negative spread between the bonds narrowed to 24 basis points from a negative spread of 25 basis points on Thursday.
Analysts said a stronger Canadian dollar helped offset some of the damage from the improved employment numbers, especially at the long end of the bond market.
Canada's dollar closed at C$1.3701 (US$0.7298) on Friday from C$1.3733 (US$0.7282) at Thursday's close.
"The real issue for the bond market today is the obvious strength of the Canadian economy," said Doug Porter, senior economist with Canadian-based brokerage Nesbitt Burns.
"This morning's employment numbers speak for themselves. Obviously, the economy is in the midst of a very powerful growth phase," Porter added.
Long-term bonds also benefited from speculation that Canada's improved fiscal ledger would reduce the number of new bond issues and force a subsequent contraction in supply to the bond markets.
Nesbitt Burns reported on Friday that Canada had stopped new borrowing for the first time since 1974 and the federal government was issuing no new bonds a year earlier than expected.
"You're going to see new issuance of Canadian bonds basically dry up over the course of the next year," Porter said.
"They're shutting off the taps on supply suddenly, yet the demand for fixed-income products is not going to change radically. The adjusting factor will be lower interest rates," Porter said
"It should make the kinds of gains we've seen in bonds the last couple of years a permanent feature," Porter added.
Canada's benchmark 30-year long bond rose C$0.62 to C$118.91 to yield 6.549 percent.
The U.S. 30-year bond gained 15/32 to yield 6.53 percent.
The spread between the two benchmark bonds moved to a spread of two basis points, the same as at the close on Thursday.
The three-month cash T-bill yielded 3.16 percent against its U.S. equivalent, which yielded 5.12 percent.
((Paul Simao, Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8104))
